name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Saturday 18 February 1984

clue.text: Certainly last month the editor came in lazily . ..

indicators.note: something that comes in enters the inside of another word

blocks.note: December is the last month of the year; Dec is its abbreviation
a synonym, which takes the inserted letters
ED is the usual abbreviation for editor

explanation.surface: Last month the editor surely strolled in late and loafing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lazily' looks like part of the definition but is wordplay; the dots link the surface on to the next clue only.
explanation.definitionFit: Decidedly means unquestionably or definitely, matching certainly as a sentence adverb.

clue.text: . . . wandered to the Turk's.' Head and got entangled

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: the opening letter of Turk's
to ravel is to tangle

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue: the editor drifted to the Turk's Head pub and got mixed up.
explanation.walkthrough: Ravel oddly means both to tangle and to untangle; here it is to tangle.
explanation.definitionFit: Travelled means journeyed from place to place, close to roamed or wandered.

clue.text: Spare list

blocks.note: first meaning: thin, with no excess
second meaning: to tilt to one side, as a ship does

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like a list of spare parts; 'list' is the verb a ship does when it tilts.
explanation.definitionFit: Lean describes a spare, thin frame, and to lean is to tilt or incline like a listing ship.

clue.text: A twisting convoy almost above the town took one in

indicators.note: almost all of the word is kept, so its final letter goes
in a down clue, what sits above comes first in the answer
'took ... in' means admitted inside, so the town word holds the next piece within it
completes 'took ... in': the following word goes inside the town word

blocks.note: the word without its last letter
Luton is a town north of London, home of an airport
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A convoy wound its way over the hill above town and picked someone up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the town' is vague: Luton, a town north of London, is simply the one that fits.
explanation.definitionFit: A convolution is a coil, twist or fold, as in the convolutions of the brain.

clue.text: Man standing up gets in the way of a forceful blow

indicators.note: in a down clue standing up means read from the bottom, i.e. backwards
getting in means going inside the next word

blocks.note: a man's name, written backwards
St is the abbreviation for street, a way

explanation.surface: A man rising blocks the path of a punch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Blow' suggests a punch; it is breath blown hard through the nose.
explanation.definitionFit: A snort is a sudden noisy blast of breath forced out through the nostrils.

clue.text: Paced around to find the tree centre

indicators.note: the centre of a phrase is its inside, so the answer lies within the opening words

blocks.note: runs from inside the first word into the second

explanation.surface: Someone walking circles round a tree, searching for its middle.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition sits mid-clue, unusually: the opening words hold the answer, and 'centre' at the end says to look in their middle.
explanation.definitionFit: The cedar is a large evergreen conifer, prized for its fragrant reddish timber.

clue.text: A third person with skill and courage

blocks.note: 'he' is a third-person pronoun
art is skill, as in the art of persuasion

explanation.surface: Someone else entirely who is both talented and brave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A third person' reads as a stranger; in grammar it is the pronoun he.
explanation.definitionFit: Heart is used to mean bravery or spirit, as in 'take heart' or 'lose heart'.

clue.text: Told about firm get ting 'ounded

blocks.note: re is Latin-derived 'concerning'
Co. is the abbreviation for company, a firm
getting hounded is being hunted; the apostrophe asks for the dropped H too, so it is 'unted

explanation.surface: A Cockney grumbling that the firm keeps on at him, related about the company.
explanation.walkthrough: The dropped H of 'ounded is a hint to drop the H from the synonym as well, Cockney fashion. The gap in 'get ting' is the newspaper scan's.
explanation.definitionFit: To recount a story is to narrate it, so recounted means told.

clue.text: The riddle of the Susie Veronica

indicators.note: 'of' here means 'made out of', so the answer is taken from inside the following words

blocks.note: spans the end of the first name and the start of the second

explanation.surface: A puzzle concerning two women called Susie and Veronica.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Riddle' looks like a puzzle, but it is the old word for a coarse sieve.
explanation.definitionFit: A riddle is a large coarse-meshed sieve for soil or grain, a sense also used as a verb.

clue.text: Runs a live broadcast world-wide

indicators.note: broadcast seed is scattered about, so these letters are strewn into a new order

blocks.note: the fodder, every letter used

explanation.surface: A live programme is transmitted all round the globe.
explanation.definitionFit: Universal means applying everywhere, synonymous with global in reach.

clue.text: The highway's getting most unsuitable

definitions.note: the clue's superlative is looser than the plain adjective answer

blocks.note: the M1 is Britain's first motorway; with 's it is M1'S, the 1 read as I
getting rich is becoming rich

explanation.surface: Complaining that the main road keeps getting worse.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is the motorway from London to Leeds, and the digit 1 stands in for the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: Misbecoming is an old word for unbecoming: improper or not fitting the occasion.

clue.text: Poor li'l me with a brace may be taken back

indicators.note: something poor is in bad shape, so these letters are knocked out of order

blocks.note: the fodder; 'with' only joins the two parts

explanation.surface: A pitiful child in teeth braces hoping someone will take them home.
explanation.definitionFit: Something reclaimable can be recovered or demanded back, the same idea as able to be retrieved.

clue.text: Excuse for a little party? I'm on!

blocks.note: taken as written
Lib, short for the Liberal party
I'm reads as the letter I

explanation.surface: Someone eagerly accepting an invitation to a small party as a pretext.
explanation.walkthrough: 'little party' is not a small gathering but an abbreviated political party; 'on' only says I goes on the end.
explanation.definitionFit: An alibi is a plea of being elsewhere, and loosely any excuse.

clue.text: Fed up with one terribly nice model wanting ...

indicators.note: in a down clue 'up' means the word is read from bottom to top
something done terribly is done badly, so these letters are jumbled

blocks.note: taken as written, then reversed
Roman numeral one
taken as written, then jumbled
the Model T Ford

explanation.surface: Tired of a dreadfully sweet model who keeps wanting things, leading into the next clue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Model' gives T from Henry Ford's famous Model T car.
explanation.definitionFit: Wanting in the sense of lacking or falling short means deficient.

clue.text: . . .to deny getting help over breaking into fame

indicators.note: over in a down clue means turned upside down, so read backwards
breaking into somewhere means getting inside it

blocks.note: repute is renown, fame
a synonym, turned backwards

explanation.surface: Continuing: a model refuses to be helped into the limelight.
explanation.definitionFit: To repudiate is to reject or refuse to acknowledge, a stronger form of denying.

clue.text: A song to delight

blocks.note: first meaning: a part-song for unaccompanied voices
second meaning: joy, merriment

explanation.surface: Singing something to give people pleasure.
explanation.definitionFit: A glee is an English part-song for several voices, and glee also means joyful high spirits.

clue.text: Constructed some form of Liberal Trade Union

indicators.note: putting letters into some other form means rearranging them

blocks.note: Lib is the short form of Liberal
TU is the abbreviation for trade union

explanation.surface: Political talk about cobbling together a Liberal-union alliance.
explanation.definitionFit: Built and constructed are synonyms, both the past tense of putting something up.

clue.text: She's right, as always

blocks.note: the first woman, a crossword's usual 'she'
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Praise for a woman who is never wrong.
explanation.definitionFit: Ever means at all times, as in 'ever hopeful', a synonym of always.

clue.text: One Scotsman, with money owing after car accident, is bitter

indicators.note: a car accident leaves the vehicle mangled, so its letters come out in a broken order

blocks.note: taken as written, then mangled
Roman numeral one
'mon' (man) is the stock Scots word in crosswords
IOUs are written acknowledgements of debts

explanation.surface: A Scot left in debt after crashing his car feels resentful.
explanation.walkthrough: An IOU ('I owe you') is a note promising repayment, so their plural stands for debts.
explanation.definitionFit: Acrimonious means full of resentment and harsh words, as bitter does of a quarrel.

clue.text: The last word - last word - to improve

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter

blocks.note: amen is said at the end of a prayer
the closing letter of word

explanation.surface: An editor insisting the final word must be changed for the better.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated phrase is used twice over: first as a whole, then for its final letter only.
explanation.definitionFit: To amend a text or law is to correct or make it better.

clue.text: Be on top of the wave even without a ring

definitions.text: Be on top of the wave

indicators.note: 'without' in its old sense means outside, so one word wraps round the other

blocks.note: even and level ground is flat
the letter O is ring-shaped

explanation.surface: A surfer who stays upright even without a ring buoy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' looks like 'lacking'; here it is the old 'outside'.
explanation.definitionFit: To float is to rest on the surface of water rather than sink.

clue.text: Mum let one out for a fee

indicators.note: 'out' can mean wrong or disordered, so these letters are put out of their order

blocks.note: the fodder, every letter used

explanation.surface: Mother rented out a room in exchange for payment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'let one out' reads as renting, which makes 'fee' seem natural; 'out' is in fact the rearranging signal.
explanation.definitionFit: An emolument is a salary, fee or payment received for work or office.

clue.text: Want to be north, up-river

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means the word is read bottom to top

blocks.note: N is the abbreviation for north
the Dee is a river in Britain

explanation.surface: Wishing to head north, travelling upstream.
explanation.definitionFit: Need and want both mean to lack or require something.

clue.text: Restriction that is the extreme of endurances

blocks.note: first meaning: a cap or bound
second meaning: the furthest point anyone can stand

explanation.surface: A rule that marks how far people can be pushed.
explanation.walkthrough: The plural 'endurances' is odd; it only means the point beyond which no one can endure.
explanation.definitionFit: A limit is a restriction such as a speed cap, and 'the limit' is the furthest point that can be borne.

clue.text: In the round, Aunt Edna is intrepid

indicators.note: 'in' says the answer sits inside the words that follow

blocks.note: runs from inside the first word to inside the third, ignoring the comma and spaces

explanation.surface: Aunt Edna, the stock timid theatregoer, bravely attends a play staged in the round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the' is padding to make 'In the round' read as theatre-in-the-round. Aunt Edna was playwright Terence Rattigan's name for the conventional middle-class playgoer.
explanation.definitionFit: Undaunted means not discouraged by danger or difficulty, which is what intrepid describes.

clue.text: Flies in retreat from most anglers

indicators.note: 'from' means taken out of the words that follow
retreating means going backwards, so the letters are read right to left

blocks.note: spans the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: Insects back away from fishermen, who know flies well.
explanation.definitionFit: Gnats are small two-winged insects, a kind of fly.
